title: On-call & Incident Response Playbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary

This playbook defines Redwood Inference's on-call and incident response processes, runbooks for common failure modes, postmortem expectations, on-call rotation rules, game day guidance, and templates for status page and customer communications. It is intended for engineers, SREs, support, and product owners who participate in incident handling and follow-up.

Scope

- Production and staging environments that directly affect customer-facing inference APIs (hosted, dedicated control plane, and private-delivered control planes).
- Covers Sev1 / Sev2 / Sev3 incidents (definitions below), on-call responsibilities, escalation, communications, and post-incident actions.

Table of contents

1) Roles & responsibilities
2) Incident lifecycle and severity definitions
3) Escalation matrix and contact table
4) Runbooks (examples)
5) Postmortem and RCA process
6) On-call rotations and handoffs
7) Game days and exercises
8) Status page & customer comms templates
9) Related tools and references

1) Roles & responsibilities

- Incident Commander (IC): Owns coordination, timeline, and communications until incident is declared resolved. Typically the on-call primary unless handed off.
- Primary on-call (Pager): First responder; responsible for initial diagnosis and mitigation.
- Secondary on-call (Backup): Provides escalation support, handles paging overflow, and steps in for long incidents.
- Tech Lead / Service Owner: Provides architecture context and authorizes code/infra changes.
- SRE Lead / Platform Ops: Executes infra-level mitigations (capacity, routing, failover).
- Customer Success / Support: Coordinates customer-facing messaging for impacted customers.
- Postmortem author: Drafts the postmortem with factual timeline and action items within 72 hours of incident resolution.

2) Incident lifecycle and severity definitions

Severity levels (examples):
- Sev1 (Critical): Major outage with widespread customer impact, > 50% error rate or complete service unavailability for customer-facing API endpoints. Response: immediate paging to primary + secondary and on-call leadership. SLOs at risk.
- Sev2 (High): Significant degradation impacting a subset of customers or features (e.g., high latency for long requests, model-serving partial failures). Response: page primary, possible escalation.
- Sev3 (Medium): Low-impact errors, degraded metrics without customer-facing outage (background jobs failing). Response: ticket and async handling; on-call may be engaged if trend escalates.

Incident lifecycle (high level):
1. Detection: Alert triggers based on SLO/SLA thresholds, synthetic tests, or user reports.
2. Triage: Primary acknowledges page within defined target (see SLOs & paging below) and assesses severity.
3. Mitigation: Implement short-term fixes to reduce impact (traffic reroute, scale-up, fallback models, circuit breakers).
4. Recovery: Restore normal service and confirm with verification tests.
5. Post-incident: Runbook review, postmortem, action items, and monitor for regressions.

Paging & acknowledgement targets
- Pager to primary: alert -> 2 minutes to acknowledge for Sev1; 10 minutes for Sev2.
- Escalation if no ack: after 2 minutes (Sev1) escalate to secondary; after 15 minutes (Sev2) escalate to on-call leadership.

3) Escalation matrix and contact table

Escalation matrix (plain table):
| Role | Primary contact method | Escalation window | Notes |
|------|------------------------|-------------------|-------|
| Primary on-call | Pager / Slack @oncall-primary | Immediate (2m for Sev1) | First responder |
| Secondary on-call | Pager / Slack @oncall-secondary | After primary no-ack or needs backup |
| SRE Lead | Slack + phone | After 10m of unresolved Sev1 | Coordinates cross-team mitigations |
| Platform Ops | Slack + paging policy | During capacity/infra incidents | Executes infra mitigations |
| Engineering Manager | Slack + Email | Business-impacting >30m | Enables org-level escalations |

Important links and pages:
- PagerDuty schedules: /schedules/oncall-primary
- Status page: status.redwood.example.com
- Incident runbooks folder: confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks

4) Runbooks (examples)

Runbook: High 5xx rate on inference API
- Symptom: 5xx errors spike > 10% across p95/p50; synthetic health checks failing.
- Immediate checks (10 minutes):
  1. Confirm alert on Grafana / Datadog: errors by service, region, and model.
  2. Check ingress/load balancer health and recent deploys (CI/CD jobs) in the last 30 minutes.
  3. Confirm service logs for OOMs, rate-limiting, or authentication errors.
- Mitigations (ordered):
  1. Fail open to a lightweight fallback model (if configured) via routing policy.
  2. Scale up pool capacity (autoscaling policy override) for affected model serving groups.
  3. Temporarily disable non-essential batch jobs that consume GPUs.
  4. If problem localized to specific model version, route traffic to previous pinned version.
- Verification: Run synthetic requests and confirm error rate < 1% for 15 minutes.
- Post-action: Note exact mitigation in timeline for postmortem and roll back any emergency changes after stabilization.

Runbook: Persistent model OOM on GPU during decode
- Symptom: Worker process crashes with CUDA OOM or model fails to allocate KV cache.
- Immediate checks:
  1. Inspect worker logs for OOM stack traces and which tensor allocation failed.
  2. Check recent changes to quantization profile or model size.
  3. Check concurrent request volumes and sequence length distribution around the time of failure.
- Mitigations:
  1. Drop to a lower-max-seq-length profile via routing policy for new requests.
  2. Re-route some traffic to smaller/quantized model variant.
  3. Drain and restart failing worker nodes (graceful request drain).
  4. If recurring, open a change to adjust batching heuristics and KV cache allocation.
- Verification: Confirm stable worker pool for 30 minutes with no new OOMs; report findings in timeline.

Runbook: Authentication/authorization failures for control plane APIs
- Symptom: Errors like 401/403 across many endpoints; customers report token rejections.
- Immediate checks:
  1. Confirm KMS/HSM service availability and recent key rotations.
  2. Check auth service health and ingress certificates.
  3. Look for recent deploys of the auth-service or config changes in secrets manager.
- Mitigations:
  1. Roll back recent auth-service deploy if correlated.
  2. Re-issue fallback signing key if key-rotation process failed and documented fallback allowed. Coordinate with security.
  3. Route customer requests to a read-only fallback where possible and notify customers.
- Verification: Synthetic token exchange flow succeeding end-to-end.

Runbook checklist & best practices
- Keep runbooks short, prescriptive, and actionable (under 1-2 pages).
- State who owns the runbook and the last-reviewed date.
- Include commands, dashboards, and exact paths to logs.
- After any emergency remediation, update runbook with any missing steps.

5) Postmortem and RCA process

When to write a postmortem:
- All Sev1 incidents must have a postmortem published within 72 hours.
- Sev2 incidents reviewed within 1 week and postmortem required if customer impact or repeated incidents.
- Sev3 incidents: triaged and included in monthly reliability reports if recurring.

Postmortem template (required sections):
1. Title: YYYY-MM-DD - Short description (e.g., 2026-02-10 - Inference API Sev1 outage)
2. Summary: One-paragraph summary of impact and duration.
3. Timeline: Chronological bullet list with timestamps (UTC) and actor/command.
4. Impact: Metrics (requests affected, % of traffic, customers impacted, downtime minutes).
5. Root cause: Clear technical root cause statement.
6. Contributing factors: Secondary issues that increased blast radius.
7. Resolution & mitigations: Immediate remediation steps and long-term fixes.
8. Action items: Assigned owner, ETA, priority, and verification plan.
9. Lessons learned: Operational and process changes recommended.
10. Approvals / reviewers: List of reviewers and approvers.

Postmortem ownership & SLAs:
- Postmortem author must be the incident commander or designated reviewer.
- Draft ready: within 48 hours; published: within 72 hours for Sev1.
- Action items tracked in issue tracker with owners and due dates.

6) On-call rotations and handoffs

Schedule and shifts
- Primary rotation: 1 week (Mon-Sun) by default.
- Secondary rotation: 2 weeks aligned with primary schedule but staggered across teams to ensure coverage.
- Night/weekend coverage: follow same schedule; ensure secondary is aware for extended incidents.
- Shift length: standard on-call increment is weekly to reduce context-switching. Short-term emergency swaps allowed with manager approval.

Handoff checklist (to run at shift change)
1. Update the on-call status page and Slack presence (e.g., set status to "on-call").
2. Review open incidents and their current state; update the timeline in each incident doc.
3. Confirm alerting: run a test alert and verify the on-call receives it.
4. Verify access: ensure keys, VPN, runbook links, and privileged accounts are working.
5. Note any ongoing game-days or maintenance windows.

On-call etiquette & burnout prevention
- Respect guaranteed primary rest periods after handling a Sev1: no non-urgent meetings for remainder of the day when possible.
- Use secondary as first escalation for prolonged incidents; rotate owners of long-running action items.
- Encourage 'buddy' handoffs for incidents spanning multiple rotations.

7) Game days and exercises

Purpose
- Validate runbooks, paging, and cross-team coordination in a controlled environment. Game days surface gaps in automation, runbook clarity, and handoffs.

Quarterly game day plan (example)
- Prep (2 weeks before): Define scenario, targets (objectives), and participants. Notify support and product teams.
- Execution (1 day): Simulate a Sev2/Sev1 event (e.g., model-serving degradation with auth degradation) and require teams to follow the incident lifecycle.
- Debrief (1-2 days after): Publish findings, update runbooks, and create action items.

Game day checklist
- Verify alert routing and escalation.
- Time-to-acknowledge measurements.
- Validate status page updates and customer comms.
- Practice postmortem drafting within 48 hours.

8) Status page & customer comms templates

Status page content guidelines
- Keep customer-facing statements concise, non-technical, and honest about impact and ETA for next update.
- Internal status entries should include technical notes for support and engineering.

Customer-facing status update (template)
- Title: [Incident] Inference API degraded - {short impact note}
- Body (initial update):
  We are investigating increased error rates impacting inference requests for customers in {region}. Our engineers are actively diagnosing the issue. Impact: some requests returning errors or experiencing elevated latency. We will provide another update within 30 minutes or when we have a remediation.
- Body (update):
  Engineers have identified {high-level cause or affected subsystem}. Mitigation in progress: {what we are doing at a high level}. Estimated time to resolution: {ETA if known, else "TBD"}.
- Body (resolution):
  The issue has been resolved as of {timestamp UTC}. Root cause: {one-sentence root cause summary}. Mitigation: {short-term mitigation applied}. Next steps: {postmortem link and planned long-term fixes}. If you experienced user-impact during {window}, please contact support@redwood.example.com with your request id and timestamps.

Internal incident comms (Slack & email template)
- Subject: [INCIDENT][Sev1] Inference API - {short summary}
- Body:
  Impact: {metrics and scope}
  IC: {name} | Primary: {name} | Secondary: {name}
  Current status: {Investigating / Mitigating / Resolved}
  Action taken: {list}
  Next update: {time}
  Postmortem owner: {name}

9) Related tools and references

- PagerDuty runbooks and schedule links:https://pagerduty.example.com/schedules
- Status page (public): https://status.redwood.example.com
- Incident tracker board: Jira: INCD-Board (internal)
- Monitoring dashboards: Grafana -> "Inference API Overview"; Datadog -> "Model Serving Errors"
- Runbook source folder: confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks

Appendix: Quick-check escalation decision tree

1. Alert fires -> Primary acknowledges?
  - Yes -> Triage-> Mitigate-> Recover-> Postmortem if Sev1
  - No -> Escalate to secondary after configured window; if still no ack, page SRE lead
2. Recovery achieved?
  - Yes -> Run verification tests -> Close incident -> Start post-incident work
  - No -> Consider wider escalations (manager, cross-region fallback, external capacity)

Document maintenance
- Owner: eng-sre team with engineering as the overall owner.
- Review cadence: runbooks reviewed quarterly; full playbook reviewed semi-annually or after any Sev1 incident.

Contact list (for internal use)
- On-call roster & Slack handles: see PagerDuty schedule page.
- Emergency phone tree: listed in PagerDuty contact entries (restricted access).

This playbook should be used as the source of truth during incidents. If you encounter gaps, raise a change request to update the specific runbook or this playbook and notify the on-call leadership.
